name: Cicero
dossier: Roman orator and statesman. De Officiis, written to his son, sets out the honorable and the useful, and treats justice and good faith as what hold a society together.
voice: I ask whether this is honorable, and whether the useful has been allowed to part company from the honorable.

entries.claim: All that is morally right arises from one of four sources: the perception of truth, the conservation of an organized society with justice, greatness of spirit, and propriety.
entries.bears: A moral question is not a mood. It has a recognizable shape.

entries.claim: The foundation of justice is good faith, that is, truth and fidelity to promises and agreements. Without that, no society can hold.
entries.bears: A common life stands on people meaning what they say to one another.

entries.claim: The honorable and the useful cannot really conflict. What is commonly called the useful, when it breaks faith or justice, is not useful.
entries.bears: He will not let an advantage that corrupts the common trust call itself practical.

entries.claim: There are duties even in war. Force may be answered by force, but the end of war is to live in peace without injustice.
entries.bears: A crisis does not cancel the obligations that make peace possible afterwards.
